{{distinguish|n-group (category theory)}}
In mathematical [[finite group theory]], an '''N-group''' is a group all of whose [[local subgroup]]s (that is, the [[normalizer]]s of nontrivial [[p-group|''p''-subgroups]]) are [[solvable group]]s. The non-solvable ones were classified by [[John G. Thompson|Thompson]] during his work on finding all the minimal finite simple groups.

==Simple N-groups==

The simple N-groups were classified by {{harvs|txt|last=Thompson|year1=1968|year2=1970|year3=1971|year4=1973|year5=1974|year6=1974b}} in a series of 6 papers totaling about 400 pages.

The simple N-groups consist of the [[special linear group]]s PSL<sub>2</sub>(''q''), PSL<sub>3</sub>(3), the [[Suzuki groups]] Sz(2<sup>2''n''+1</sup>),  the [[unitary group]] U<sub>3</sub>(3), the [[alternating group]] ''A''<sub>7</sub>, the [[Mathieu group]] M<sub>11</sub>, and the [[Tits group]]. (The Tits group was overlooked in Thomson's original announcement in 1968, but Hearn pointed out that it was also a simple N-group.) More generally Thompson showed that any non-solvable N-group is a subgroup of Aut(''G'') containing ''G'' for some simple N-group ''G''.

{{Harvtxt|Gorenstein|Lyons|1976}} generalized Thompson's theorem to the case of groups where all 2-local subgroups are solvable. The only extra simple groups that appear are the unitary groups U<sub>3</sub>(''q'').

==Proof==

{{harvtxt|Gorenstein|1980|loc=16.5}} gives a summary of Thompson's classification of N-groups. 

The primes dividing the order of the group are divided into four classes π<sub>1</sub>, π<sub>2</sub>, π<sub>3</sub>, π<sub>4</sub> as follows
*π<sub>1</sub> is the set of primes ''p'' such that a [[Sylow group|Sylow]] ''p''-subgroup is nontrivial and cyclic.
*π<sub>2</sub> is the set of primes ''p'' such that a Sylow ''p''-subgroup ''P'' is non-cyclic but SCN<sub>3</sub>(''P'') is empty.
*π<sub>3</sub> is the set of primes ''p'' such that a Sylow ''p''-subgroup ''P'' has SCN<sub>3</sub>(''P'') nonempty and normalizes a nontrivial abelian subgroup of order prime to ''p''.
*π<sub>4</sub> is the set of primes ''p'' such that a Sylow ''p''-subgroup ''P'' has SCN<sub>3</sub>(''P'') nonempty but does not normalize a nontrivial abelian subgroup of order prime to ''p''.

The proof is subdivided into several cases depending on which of these four classes the prime 2 belongs to, and also on an integer ''e'', which is the largest [[integer]] for which there is an [[elementary abelian]] subgroup of rank ''e'' normalized by a nontrivial 2-subgroup intersecting it trivially. 

*{{harvtxt|Thompson|1968}} Gives a general introduction, stating the main theorem and proving many preliminary lemmas.
*{{harvtxt|Thompson|1970}} characterizes the groups ''E''<sub>2</sub>(3) and ''S''<sub>4</sub>(3) (in Thompson's notation; these are the exceptional group ''G''<sub>2</sub>(3) and the symplectic group ''Sp''<sub>4</sub>(3)) which are not N-groups but whose characterizations are needed in the proof of the main theorem.
*{{harvtxt|Thompson|1971}} covers the case where 2∉π<sub>4</sub>. Theorem 11.2 shows that if 2∈π<sub>2</sub> then the group is PSL<sub>2</sub>(''q''), M<sub>11</sub>, ''A''<sub>7</sub>, U<sub>3</sub>(3), or PSL<sub>3</sub>(3).  The possibility that 2∈π<sub>3</sub> is ruled out by showing that any such group must be a C-group and using Suzuki's classification of C-groups to check that none of the groups found by Suzuki satisfy this condition.
*{{harvtxt|Thompson|1973}} and {{harvtxt|Thompson|1974}} cover the cases when 2∈π<sub>4</sub> and ''e''≥3, or ''e''=2. He shows that either ''G'' is a [[C-group]] so a Suzuki group, or satisfies his characterization of the groups ''E''<sub>2</sub>(3) and ''S''<sub>4</sub>(3) in his second paper, which are not N-groups.
*{{harvtxt|Thompson|1974}} covers the case when 2∈π<sub>4</sub> and ''e''=1, where the only possibilities are that ''G'' is  a [[C-group]] or the [[Tits group]].

==Consequences==
A '''minimal simple group''' is a non-cyclic simple group all of whose proper subgroups are solvable. 
The complete list of minimal finite simple groups is given as follows {{harvtxt|Thompson|1968|loc=corollary 1}}
*PSL<sub>2</sub>(2<sup>''p''</sup>), ''p'' a prime.
*PSL<sub>2</sub>(3<sup>''p''</sup>), ''p'' an odd prime.
*PSL<sub>2</sub>(''p''), ''p''&nbsp;>&nbsp;3 a prime congruent to 2 or 3 mod&nbsp;5
*Sz(2<sup>''p''</sup>), ''p'' an odd prime.
*PSL<sub>3</sub>(3)

In other words a non-cyclic [[finite simple group]] must have a [[subquotient]] isomorphic to one of these groups.
